name: Evening primrose oil

lead: Evening primrose oil is pressed from the seeds of Oenothera biennis, a North American plant, and is rich in linoleic acid and gamma-linolenic acid (GLA). People take it as a supplement or apply it to dry, eczema-prone or hormonally breakout-prone skin to get calmer, less dry-looking skin.

GLA is an omega-6 fatty acid the body converts to prostaglandin precursors, and proponents argue this supports skin barrier and inflammatory balance. It has been studied for atopic eczema, breast pain and menopausal symptoms; a Cochrane review found no effect on eczema, and the US NCCIH describes the evidence as insufficient for any medical condition.

paras: It is mostly taken as capsules, with some people applying the oil or using skincare products containing it. People commonly use it daily for several weeks or months and pair it with a moisturiser routine.

Described as likely safe at recommended amounts, with headache and nausea reported. It may raise bleeding risk, and sources advise caution in people with seizure disorders or mania and in pregnancy or breastfeeding.

chain: Support for skin barrier and inflammation
angle.text: Evening primrose oil supplies gamma-linolenic acid, which proponents say supports the skin barrier and calms inflammation, so it is taken or applied for dry, eczema-prone or breakout-prone skin. Reviews of its use for eczema find insufficient evidence.

lead: Evening primrose oil (EPO) is a vegetable oil obtained from the seeds of the common evening primrose, Oenothera biennis, a North American plant that became naturalised across much of the world.[1] The seeds contain about 24 percent oil, rich in the polyunsaturated fatty acids linoleic acid and gamma-linolenic acid (GLA).[1]

Its main commercial use is as an oral dietary supplement, and it is also used in some skin products.[1] It has been examined in trials for atopic eczema, breast pain, menopausal symptoms and other conditions. A Cochrane review reported in reference sources found no effect on eczema, and the US National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health (NCCIH) is cited as finding the evidence insufficient to support use for any medical condition.[1][2]

paras: Evening primrose (Oenothera biennis) is native to eastern and central North America, was named by Linnaeus in 1753 and reached Europe in the early 17th century as a garden ornamental. The seeds are about a quarter oil, and the oil contains linoleic acid and gamma-linolenic acid (GLA), the fatty acids for which it is sold as a dietary supplement. [1]
Indigenous peoples used the plant as food and medicine, with leaves and stems applied to skin, digestive and throat complaints, and the roots, leaves and buds were eaten. [1]

Indigenous peoples of North America used the plant as food and traditional medicine, and it reached Europe in the early 17th century as an ornamental garden plant.[1] Its modern use centres on the oil from its seeds as a supplement.[1]

Wikipedia's gamma-linolenic acid page describes evening primrose as a folk remedy in Europe known as king's cure-all, and reports that in 1919 Heiduschka and Lüft extracted the oil from the seeds and described an unusual linolenic acid, which they named gamma-linolenic acid, with its exact structure characterised later by Riley. [3] In the UK, the Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency withdrew marketing authorisations for evening primrose oil as an eczema treatment in 2002. [3]

EPO is promoted for skin health because of its GLA content, and it has been tested mainly in eczema rather than in cosmetic outcomes such as wrinkles or complexion. A systematic review of atopic eczema treatments assessed evening primrose oil among them.[4] Memorial Sloan Kettering's patient page describes some data suggesting improved skin moisture and reduced water loss through the skin in healthy adults, and a possible role in preventing dry lips in people taking isotretinoin, while calling human evidence for skin conditions limited and mixed. [5]

Complementary-medicine reviews have assessed EPO for menopausal vasomotor symptoms, and the North American Menopause Society position statement addressed such treatments.[6][2] It has also been used or reviewed for breast pain, diabetic neuropathy, premenstrual symptoms and inflammatory bowel disease, with the Mayo Clinic cited as finding no good evidence for eczema, diabetic neuropathy or premenstrual syndrome.[1][7][8]

Reference sources describe EPO as likely safe at recommended amounts. Oral use may cause headache or nausea, and it may increase bleeding risk, which is relevant to people with bleeding disorders or those taking drugs that affect bleeding.[1] The Mayo Clinic is cited as advising caution for people with seizure disorders or mania and in pregnancy and breastfeeding.[1]

Reviews of herb-drug interactions and of complementary medicine use in cancer patients have discussed evening primrose among herbal products with potential interaction concerns, and laboratory work has tested herbal components for effects on cytochrome P450 enzymes.[9][10][11]

Memorial Sloan Kettering lists stomach pain, nausea, headache, indigestion and softer stools among common effects, and notes increased bleeding risk with anticoagulant or antiplatelet drugs, possible increases in levels of some antiretrovirals, and caution in pregnancy and with hormone-sensitive cancers because some commercial products contain phytoestrogens. Case reports include lipoid pneumonia after long-term use and bruising in a newborn whose mother had used it before delivery. [5]

GLA, an omega-6 fatty acid, is a precursor of prostaglandin-type signalling molecules, which is the basis on which proponents suggest anti-inflammatory and skin-barrier effects. Studies comparing polyunsaturated fatty acid supplements have also reported effects of other fatty acids on immune cell function, for example fish oil and eicosapentaenoic acid.[12][13]

The body makes GLA from linoleic acid via the enzyme delta-6-desaturase, and activity of that enzyme can fall with age or dietary deficiencies. GLA is converted to dihomo-gamma-linolenic acid, an eicosanoid precursor that leads to prostaglandin E1 and cannot form leukotrienes, which is the basis of proponents' anti-inflammatory rationale. [3] Evening primrose oil provides GLA at roughly 8 to 14 percent, compared with about 15 to 20 percent in blackcurrant seed oil and 17 to 25 percent in borage seed oil, which are used as alternative GLA supplements. [3]

People take EPO capsules, or apply the oil, hoping for softer, less dry and less irritated skin, with the chain running from GLA to anti-inflammatory prostaglandin precursors to calmer, better-hydrated skin. Reviews of dietary interventions for atopic eczema in children have examined fatty-acid supplements among other options. [14]

Reference sources summarise the research on eczema: a Cochrane review found no effect of primrose oil on eczema, and the Mayo Clinic reports a lack of good evidence for eczema, premenstrual syndrome and diabetic neuropathy. [1] Trials in breast pain, premenstrual symptoms and menopausal hot flushes have also been reviewed. [15][16]

Forms include oral capsules and, less commonly, oil applied to skin or added to creams. Users commonly pair it with other skin-supporting routines, and some take it for hormonal-skin or cyclic breast symptoms, areas for which Memorial Sloan Kettering summarises evidence as mixed. [5]

Trial registrations include EPO for breast-feeding pain (n=80),[17] induction of labour,[18] second-trimester missed miscarriage,[19][20] a vitamin E and EPO comparison for cyclical breast pain (n=82),[21] menopausal symptoms compared with lavender,[22] and a Phase 4 study of the prescription GLA product Epogam in atopic dermatitis (n=23).[23] A systematic review of eczema treatments and reviews of complementary treatments in menopause and inflammatory bowel disease have summarised randomised evidence.[4][6][8] Reference sources report that a Cochrane review found no benefit for eczema.[1] No clinical studies of EPO for facial skin appearance specifically were found.

Memorial Sloan Kettering summarises small trials suggesting benefit in atopic dermatitis alongside other analyses finding no effect, mixed results for menopausal hot flashes, and no improvement in some analyses of breast pain and premenstrual symptoms, with one trial finding benefit for cyclical breast pain when combined with vitamin E. [5] A 2003 BMJ commentary on the eczema story, as summarised by Wikipedia, called for more transparency in drug-licensing research. [3]

timeline.event: Evening primrose reaches Europe as an ornamental plant.[1]
Heiduschka and Lüft extract oil from evening primrose seeds and describe gamma-linolenic acid. [3]
A Health Technology Assessment systematic review evaluates treatments for atopic eczema including EPO.[4]
A review of complementary therapies for menopausal symptoms is published.[6]
UK MHRA withdraws marketing authorisations for evening primrose oil as an eczema remedy. [3]
